law_name: Ministerial statement (البيان الوزاري) of the Salam government
description: Approved by the cabinet on 17 February 2025 and endorsed by parliament's confidence vote on 26 February 2025 (95 MPs). It states that the state alone holds weapons and decides on war and peace, commits to UN Security Council Resolution 1701, to liberating territory held by Israel through state forces, to negotiating a new IMF programme, restructuring the banks, protecting depositors, strengthening judicial independence, letting the Beirut port investigation proceed and holding municipal and parliamentary elections on schedule.
significance: The first ministerial statement in two decades with no reference to a right of 'resistance', the formula that had covered Hezbollah's arsenal.

law_name: Amendment of the banking secrecy law
description: Reform of Lebanon's banking secrecy rules adopted by parliament in April 2025, one of the IMF's prerequisites for a new programme.
significance: First of the IMF-required financial laws passed under Salam; earlier attempts had failed.

law_name: Law on the resolution and restructuring of banks, and its amendment by Law No. 71 of 10 September 2026
description: Framework for the recovery and restructuring of Lebanon's banks, most of which have been insolvent since 2019, adopted by parliament on 31 July 2025 with IMF involvement. After the IMF judged it insufficient, the government withdrew a first revision in early 2026, approved new amendments on 30 April 2026, and parliament adopted them as Law No. 71 of 10 September 2026. On 20 October 2026 the Constitutional Council, on President Aoun's appeal, annulled its Article 3 and two phrases on travel bans and immunity for bank employees.
significance: With the 'financial gap' law, one of the two central IMF requirements; the October 2026 ruling left the division of powers with the central bank unresolved.

law_name: Law on the independence of the judiciary (organisation of the ordinary courts)
description: Bill approved by the cabinet and adopted by parliament on 31 July 2025; President Aoun asked parliament to reconsider it on 5 September 2025, and an amended version was adopted on 18 December 2025. It expands judicial self-governance and the election of judges by their peers, but according to Human Rights Watch keeps limits on judicial independence, notably on the Higher Judicial Council's power over appointments.
significance: A long-standing demand of judges, civil society and international donors; Human Rights Watch called it positive but short of guaranteeing independence.

law_name: Cabinet decisions on the state monopoly of arms (5 August 2025) and the army's plan (5 September 2025)
description: On 5 August 2025 the cabinet tasked the Lebanese army with a plan to confine weapons to six official security forces by the end of 2025; on 5 September 2025 it welcomed the army's five-phase plan, kept its details confidential and required monthly reports. The army said in January 2026 that it had completed the first phase, south of the Litani River.
significance: The first time a Lebanese cabinet formally addressed disarming Hezbollah; Hezbollah called the decision a 'grave sin'.

law_name: Draft 'financial gap' law on the distribution of losses and the repayment of deposits
description: Bill approved by the cabinet on 26 December 2025 by 13 votes to 9 and sent to parliament. It shares the losses of the 2019 crisis (about $70 billion by government estimates) between the state, the central bank, banks and depositors; deposits up to $100,000 would be repaid in full over four years, and larger ones partly in tradable bonds backed by central-bank assets. Pending in parliament as of October 2026.
significance: The IMF and the Finance Minister say a full IMF programme depends on its adoption.

law_name: Cabinet decision banning Hezbollah's military and security activities (2 March 2026)
description: Adopted at an emergency cabinet meeting hours after Hezbollah fired rockets and drones at Israel: it declares the group's military and security activities outside the law, obliges it to hand over its weapons and orders the army and security services to prevent launches from Lebanese territory and arrest those responsible.
significance: Lebanon's first formal prohibition of Hezbollah's armed activity; followed by measures against Iran's Revolutionary Guards and the expulsion of Iran's ambassador.

description: US-brokered agreement signed by the two countries' ambassadors in the presence of Secretary of State Marco Rubio, after direct negotiations that began on 14 April 2026. It links a phased Israeli withdrawal, beginning with pilot zones handed to the Lebanese army, to Hezbollah's disarmament, sets up working groups towards a peace and security agreement and includes a security annex; further Israeli withdrawals depend on benchmarks rather than a timetable.
significance: Concluded after what Al Jazeera described as the first direct negotiations between the two states since 1983; rejected by Hezbollah, with implementation stalled as of October 2026.
